messages.content: Write a Python class `LRUCache` with `get(key)` and `put(key, value)` methods that both run in O(1) time. Use `collections.OrderedDict`. The constructor takes a `capacity`; when the cache is full, `put` evicts the least recently used entry, and `get` returns -1 for a missing key. Add a short usage example at the end.

I have two PostgreSQL tables:

```sql
customers(id bigint primary key, name text, country text)
orders(id bigint primary key, customer_id bigint references customers(id), total numeric(10,2), created_at timestamptz)
```

Write a query that returns, for each country, the three customers who spent the most in 2025, with their total spend and their rank within the country. Customers with the same total should share a rank.

Write a TypeScript function `debounce` that takes a function and a delay in milliseconds and returns a debounced version of it. The returned function must keep the original parameter types, and it must have a `cancel()` method that drops a pending call. Add a JSDoc comment and a two-line example.

Explain what this regular expression accepts, piece by piece, then give two strings it accepts and two it rejects:

```
^(?=.*[A-Z])(?=.*\d)(?!.*\s)[A-Za-z\d@$!%*?&]{8,64}$
```

What does this Rust function do, and why does it need the lifetime `'a`? Keep it short.

```rust
fn longest_word<'a>(text: &'a str) -> Option<&'a str> {
    text.split_whitespace()
        .map(|w| w.trim_matches(|c: char| !c.is_alphanumeric()))
        .filter(|w| !w.is_empty())
        .max_by_key(|w| w.chars().count())
}
```
Write a short story, about 300 words, about a cartographer who discovers that one of the islands on her finest map does not exist. End it with a line of dialogue.

Write a polite but firm email to my landlord. The kitchen tap has been dripping for two weeks; I reported it on the 3rd and nobody has come. Ask for a repair date this week. Keep it under 150 words and sign it as Sam.

Summarize this passage in three sentences for a general reader.

For most of history, a lighthouse was a fire on a tower. Wood, coal and later oil lamps burned in the open or behind glass, and most of their light went everywhere except out to sea. Mirrors helped: by the late eighteenth century, polished metal reflectors shaped as parabolas gathered the light of an oil lamp into a beam. But the reflectors tarnished, and even a clean one lost about half its light. In 1822 the French physicist Augustin Fresnel proposed a lens built from concentric rings of glass prisms. Each ring bent the light by a different angle, so together they acted like one large curved lens at a fraction of its weight and thickness. The first Fresnel lens was lit at the Cordouan lighthouse in 1823, and its beam could be seen more than twenty miles away. Within fifty years the design had spread to coasts around the world. Lenses were graded by size into orders, from the first order, taller than a person, to the small sixth order used in harbours. Many of them are still in place today, although electric lamps and automatic controls replaced the keepers who once trimmed the wicks every night.
